hpi_details: 45M presents with acute onset of severe, colicky right flank pain that radiates down to his right groin. The pain started 2 hours ago. He is pacing around the room unable to find a comfortable position. He has nausea and vomiting. He noticed his urine looked slightly pink this morning.
ideas: thinks he has a kidney stone
concerns: terrified the pain will not stop
expectations: wants pain medication and a scan

investigation_events.title: Urgent renal colic investigations
investigation_events.availability_message: Urinalysis and non-contrast CT results are now available. Analgesia and antiemetic treatment should not be delayed while obtaining imaging.

results.value: 3+ blood; >50 RBC/hpf; no pyuria or nitrites
4 mm obstructing calculus at the right ureterovesical junction with mild right hydroureteronephrosis
results.note: No additional obstructing calculus is seen.

core_concepts: Classic presentation is acute, severe, colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with hematuria.
Patients typically cannot sit still, differentiating it from peritonitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming all flank pain is pyelonephritis (which typically has fever).
dangerous_errors: Missing an infected stone (fever + stone), which is a urologic emergency.
management_principles: Analgesia (NSAIDs/opioids), antiemetics, non-contrast CT abdomen/pelvis, urology consult if >10mm or infected.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Kidney Disease

reference_soap.subjective: 45M with severe, colicky right flank pain radiating to groin, nausea, and hematuria.
reference_soap.objective: Writhing in pain. Afebrile. Right CVA tenderness.
reference_soap.plan: IV Toradol, Ondansetron. Non-contrast CT Abdomen/Pelvis. Urinalysis.

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical presentation of ureteral colic and appropriate initial imaging.

teaching.one_liner: Acute severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin in a patient unable to sit still, with hematuria.

must_ask.say: Can you describe the pain, and does it move from your back down toward your groin?
Have you noticed any blood in your urine?
Have you had any fever, chills, or burning when you urinate?
Have you ever had a kidney stone before, and do you know its size?
Are you feeling nauseated or have you been vomiting with the pain?

history.answer: Doctor, please help me, I have this excruciating, agonizing pain in my right side that started suddenly, and I cannot find any position that brings relief.
It hit me completely out of the blue about two hours ago. It ramped up within minutes to this unbearable intensity.
It is centered right in my right flank and lower back on the right side, and it hasn't stayed in just one spot.
Yes, the pain shoots down from my right side straight into my right groin and towards my testicle.
It feels like intense, sharp waves of squeezing and cramping that come on fiercely and peak over several minutes.
It is easily a ten out of ten. I have never felt pain this severe in my entire life.
Nothing relieves it at all, and moving or changing positions doesn't help. That's why I can't stop pacing around the room.
No, I have never experienced anything like this before. This is the very first time.
I felt sick to my stomach as soon as the pain peaked, and I threw up clear fluid and stomach juices twice.
My bowel movements are normal. I went to the bathroom normally this morning with no diarrhea or blood, and I am still passing gas.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or shaking.
No, my eyes look clear, and my stool has looked normal brown, not pale or white.
I noticed my urine had a distinct pink tint this morning, and I feel like I need to urinate frequently, but there is no burning.
No, I have not felt dizzy, faint, or passed out, just overwhelmed by the pain.
No chest pain, palpitations, or trouble catching my breath.
history.topic: Chest pain and shortness of breath

history.answer: I had a normal light dinner last night, nothing especially greasy, and I haven't had any alcohol to drink.
I took two ibuprofen tablets about an hour ago when it started, but they didn't help in the slightest.
No, I have never had an irregular heartbeat, atrial fibrillation, or any vascular problems.
A coworker once had a kidney stone and said the pain was unbearable and radiated down low, so I wonder if I might have one.
I am terrified that this pain isn't going to let up, because I genuinely cannot bear another hour of this.
I desperately need something strong to take away the pain, and I hope we can do a scan to see what is causing it.
To be honest, I drink very little water during the day, usually just a cup of coffee in the morning and maybe one glass of water.
I was diagnosed with gout three years ago, but I don't have high blood pressure, diabetes, or kidney trouble.
I have never had any surgeries or stayed overnight in a hospital.
I take allopurinol daily for my gout prevention, and nothing else regularly.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink an occasional beer maybe once or twice a month, none recently.
I work as an accountant at an office desk, and I live with my wife and son.
My father suffered from gout, but no one in my family has had kidney disease, stones, or an aneurysm.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, pulse 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Patient is visibly distressed, diaphoretic, and restlessly pacing and writhing, unable to find a comfortable position.
Abdomen is flat and non-distended without surgical scars, visible pulsations, or skin lesions.
Normoactive bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants; no renal artery or abdominal aortic bruits.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender across all quadrants without involuntary guarding or abdominal wall rigidity.
No rebound tenderness elicited in any abdominal quadrant.
Negative Murphy sign with no tenderness or inspiratory pause on deep right upper quadrant palpation.
Negative McBurney point tenderness, negative Rovsing sign, and negative psoas and obturator signs.
Marked, sharp right costovertebral angle tenderness on gentle percussion; no left costovertebral angle tenderness.
Normal external genitalia without scrotal swelling, erythema, testicular tenderness, or inguinal hernia.
Femoral and distal pedal pulses are strong, symmetrical, and equal bilaterally with no lower extremity edema.
